overview: Bhutan is a small landlocked kingdom in the eastern Himalayas, between China and India. Its capital and largest city is Thimphu. Bhutan has never been colonised, and it became a constitutional monarchy in 2008. It is known for measuring its progress by 'Gross National Happiness' and for protecting its culture and environment.

geography.text: Bhutan rises from hot, humid lowlands in the south to high Himalayan peaks in the north. Forests cover most of the country, and steep river valleys run from north to south. Gangkhar Puensum, on the border with China, is believed to be the highest mountain in the world that has never been climbed.

subsections.title: Climate
subsections.text: Warm in the southern foothills and freezing in the high Himalaya.

subsections.title: Wildlife
subsections.text: Snow leopards, red pandas and the takin, the national animal, which looks like a goat-antelope.

history.text: Bhutan was unified in the 1600s by Zhabdrung Ngawang Namgyal, who built its great fortress-monasteries called dzongs. The Wangchuck dynasty has ruled since 1907. Bhutan stayed largely closed to the outside world until the 1960s, and in 2008 its king introduced democracy and a written constitution.

events.title: Zhabdrung arrives
events.text: Ngawang Namgyal arrives from Tibet and begins unifying Bhutan.

events.title: Wangchuck dynasty
events.text: Ugyen Wangchuck becomes the first king.

events.title: Joins the UN
events.text: Bhutan becomes a member of the United Nations.

events.title: TV and internet arrive
events.text: Bhutan allows television and the internet for the first time.

events.title: Democracy
events.text: Bhutan adopts a constitution and holds its first general election.

government.text: Bhutan is a constitutional monarchy. The King is head of state, and the Prime Minister leads the government chosen by the elected National Assembly. The King introduced democracy himself in 2008, and the constitution requires the monarch to step down at 65.

economy.text: Bhutan earns most of its money by selling hydropower electricity to India. Tourism is limited by a daily fee, so the country attracts fewer but higher-paying visitors. Bhutan measures its success by Gross National Happiness as well as by GDP.

culture.text: Bhutan is a Buddhist kingdom in the Himalayas. By law, citizens wear national dress, the gho for men and the kira for women, at work and on formal occasions. Buildings follow traditional styles. It is the only carbon-negative country in the world.

items.title: Tiger's Nest
items.text: Paro Taktsang, a monastery clinging to a cliff.

items.title: Gross National Happiness
items.text: A measure of wellbeing used to guide government decisions.

subsections.title: Food
subsections.text: Ema datshi, chillies cooked in cheese, is the national dish.

subsections.title: Music and arts
subsections.text: Thangka paintings and masked cham dances are part of Buddhist life.

subsections.title: Traditions and festivals
subsections.text: Tsechu festivals at monasteries feature days of masked dances.

sport.text: Archery is Bhutan's national sport, played at festivals with singing and dancing between shots. Football is also popular; the national team won its first ever competitive match in 2015.

items.title: Archery
items.text: Targets are set about 140 metres away.
Bhutan's football team beat Sri Lanka in World Cup qualifying.

didYouKnow: Bhutan is the world's only carbon-negative country.
Climbing Gangkhar Puensum, possibly the highest unclimbed mountain on Earth, is banned in Bhutan.

keyPeople.name: Jigme Khesar Namgyel Wangchuck
keyPeople.text: Fifth King of Bhutan, crowned in 2008.

keyPeople.name: Jigme Singye Wangchuck
keyPeople.text: Introduced the idea of Gross National Happiness.
